Surah 79, al-Nazi'at, is Meccan; its verses number forty-six.

﴿By those who drag out with violence,﴾ ﴿and those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿and those who glide along swiftly,﴾ ﴿and those who race ahead,﴾ ﴿and those who manage the affair.﴾ This is an oath by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by groups of angels who take souls out of bodies absolutely, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and Mujahid; or by the souls of the disbelievers, as stated by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Masruq. They "draw out" (yanshituna) them, meaning they bring them out of the bodies, from the expression nashata al-dalw min al-bi'r (he drew the bucket out of the well) when he pulled it out. They "glide" (yasbahuna) in extracting them like the diver who brings out what comes out of the sea. Then they "race ahead" with the souls of the disbelievers to the Fire and with the souls of the believers to the Garden, and then they "manage the affair" of their reward and punishment, by preparing them to perceive what has been readied for them of pains and pleasures. The conjunction (al-'atf), despite the unity of all of them in one reality, is for the differentiation of their essential attributes, as in the saying:

To the valiant king and the son of the brave, and the lion of the battalions in the crush,

for the indication that each of the listed attributes is among the great matters, worthy in itself of being the ground for its bearer's deserving of reverence and glorification by swearing by it, without the other attributes being joined to it. The "fa'" in the last two is to indicate that they follow what precedes them without delay, as in the saying:

Alas for Zayyaba over al-Harith, the one who rises at dawn, then the one who gains spoils, then the one who returns.

"Gharqan" is an emphatic verbal noun with its extra letters omitted, meaning: a thorough drawing out, in that it draws them from the extremities of the bodies. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it draws the soul of the disbeliever from his body from beneath every hair, from beneath the nails and the roots of the feet, then it immerses them in his body, then draws them out, until when it is about to come out it returns them into his body. This is its action with the disbelievers. It was also said: the disbeliever sees his soul at the time of extraction as though it were drowning. "Nashtan," "sabhan," and "sabqan" are likewise in the verbal-noun form. As for "amran," it is the object of "al-mudabbirat," and its indefiniteness is for awe and magnification. It is also permissible that by "al-sabihat" and what follows are meant groups of angels who glide in their passage, i.e., they hasten in it, so they race ahead to what they were commanded of worldly and otherworldly affairs. The thing sworn to is omitted, relying on the indication of what precedes it of the things sworn by and sworn to, and the indication of what follows of the states of the Resurrection, and it is "la-tub'athunna" (you will surely be resurrected). For swearing by those who take charge of drawing out souls and who undertake the management of their affairs hints that the thing sworn to is, without doubt, of the kind of those affairs. There is in this a grandeur that is not hidden. It has also been allowed that it is an oath by the stars which draw out from east to west, drawn out in their extraction, by cutting through the sphere until they descend at the farthest west, and which "nashat" from one zodiac sign to another, i.e., they come out from the "nashat" of the bull when it leaves one land for another, and they glide in the sphere so that some of them outrun others, and they thus manage a matter entrusted to them, such as the alternation of seasons, the determination of times, and the clarification of the times of worship. Since their movements from east to west are forced, and their movements from sign to sign are congenial, the first is expressed by "drawing out" and the second by "drawing out gently." Or it is an oath by the warriors themselves, or by their hands which draw the bows, drawing the arrows forth; they "draw out" with the arrow for shooting, and they "glide" over land and sea, so they race ahead to fight the enemy and thus manage its affair. Or by their horses which draw at their bridles with a pull in which the bridles are drawn out because of the length of their necks, since they are purebred; and they go out from the abode of Islam to the abode of war and glide in their running so as to race ahead to the goal, and thus manage the matter of victory and triumph. The attribution of management to them is because they are among its causes. What befits the context of the revelation, however, is the first, which is the saying of the Exalted:

﴿On the Day the quaking [blast] quakes﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied response (al-jawab al-mudmar). By "al-Rajifah" is meant the great event at which the still bodies tremble, that is, they move with violent motion and are shaken with a tremendous quaking, like the earth and the mountains. It is the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula). It has also been said that al-Rajfah is the earth and the mountains, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day the earth and the mountains quake﴾, and His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 7:

﴿Followed by the Radifa (the second blast).﴾ That is: the event that follows the first, namely the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya), which comes after it and not before that. It denotes the extended time in which the two blasts occur, and between them is forty years. The consideration of its extension, although resurrection occurs only at the second blast, is to magnify the Day by showing that it is an occasion of two great calamities: when the first occurs, no living being remains except that it dies, and when the second occurs, none remains except that it is raised up and stands. The reason for its being attributed to the first is evident. It was also said: ﴿The Day the quaking shakes﴾ is in the accusative governed by "remember" (udhkur), so the sentence becomes a resumed statement confirming the content of the implied answer, as if it were said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Remind them of the Day of the two blasts, for it is the time of their resurrection. It was also said: it is in the accusative governed by what is indicated by the words of the Exalted:

Qur'anic quotations are rendered in the requested form. Here is the translation:

﴿Hearts on that Day will be trembling﴾, i.e., on the Day when the hearts will tremble and quake. It has been said: "Hearts" is the subject (mubtada'), and "on that Day" (yawma'idhin) is related to "trembling" (wajifah), which is a qualifier (sifah) of "hearts" that makes it permissible for it to occur as a subject. And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 9:

﴿Their eyes⁠﴾ i.e., the eyes of their owners.

﴿Humbled⁠﴾ is a nominal sentence (jumla min mubtada' wa khabar) that stands as a predicate (khabar) of "hearts" (qulub). It has already been noted that the rule for an attribute (sifa) is that its attachment to the described thing should be known to the hearer, to the point that they said: attributes before knowledge of them are predicates (akhbar), and predicates after knowledge of them are attributes (sifat). Since the throbbing (wajif) of the hearts and the humbling of the eyes of their owners are equal in being known or unknown, making the first a heading for the topic, established and taken for granted, and making the second the predicate that is intended to convey information, is an arbitrary choice. Moreover, the throbbing, which is an expression for the intense agitation and disquiet of the heart from fear and dread, is more severe and more frightening than the humbling of the gaze. Thus the lesser of the two evils has been made the main element, and the greater the secondary element, something unfamiliar in speech. Also, restricting humility to hearts described by a specific attribute, one that does not imply generality or comprehensiveness, belittles the matter in a place meant to inspire awe. The correct view is therefore to say: the indefinite form of "hearts" (qulub) takes the place of a restrictive description, whether this is understood as classification (al-tanwi'), as was said, even though the opposing type is not mentioned, since the meaning extends to it, or as multiplication (al-takthir), as in "an evil that made a fanged one snarl," since magnification can be achieved by quantity just as it can by quality. It is as if it were said: many hearts on the day when the two blasts occur, throbbing, i.e., extremely agitated.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "Fearful and dreading." Al-Suddi said: "Displaced from their places," as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the hearts rise up to the throats﴾, and the saying of Allah the Exalted:

﴿They say, "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?"﴾ This is a report of what those who deny the Resurrection and reject the clear verses that speak of it say, after the matter had been established with an emphatic oath (tawkid qasami, emphasis by oath), after the mention of its terrifying preliminaries, and after what befalls hearts and eyes when they occur. That is: when it is said to them, "You will indeed be resurrected," they say, denying it and marvelling at it, "Shall we indeed be returned after our death to the hafira?" That is, to the first state, which they mean as life. This comes from their saying, "So-and-so returned along his hafira," meaning along his path, the one on which he came and so "dug" it, that is, left an impression on it by his walking. Calling it hafira although it is "dug" is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿in a pleasing life﴾, meaning a life ascribed to digging and to pleasing, or like their saying, "His day is fasting," by treating the one who receives the action as if it were the one who performs it. It was also read as fi al-hufra, and hufra here means the same as mahfura (the dug one).

(p-98) And His saying, Most High: ﴿, when we are decayed bones?﴾

﴿When we are decayed bones?﴾ is an emphatic affirmation of the denial of the return and its negation, by attributing it to a state that contradicts it. The governing element of "idhā" (when) is an implied verb indicated by "mardūdūn" (we will be returned), meaning: "When we are decayed bones, will we be returned and resurrected, while they are the furthest thing from life?" It is also read as "idhā kunnā" in the declarative form, or with the interrogative particle dropped. "Nākhira" (decayed) derives from "nakhara al-'aẓm" (the bone became hollow and decayed): one says "nakhir" and "nākhir," and it is the decayed, hollow bone through which the wind passes, so that a whistling sound (nakhīr) is heard from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 12:

﴿They said﴾ — a narration of the last part of their disbelief, branching off from their earlier disbelief. The placing of "they said" between the two (parts) may be to signal that the occurrence of this disbelief from them is not in the manner of constancy and continuity, unlike their earlier disbelief, whose occurrence from them was constant at all their times, as is indicated by its narration in the present tense. That is: they said, mockingly, pointing to what they had denied of the return to the "hafirah" (the original state of life), implying how far it is from occurring. ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾ — that is, one that brings loss, or "losing" in the sense that its adherents are losers; i.e., if it is true, then we would be losers, for our denial of it. And His exalted saying:

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, it will be but a single blast﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of an implied premise (muqaddar) which is required by their denial of the resurrection of decayed bones, which they described as "the return" (al-karrah). Since its basis (madar) was their regarding it as difficult (istis'ab), He responded to them with that, saying: Do not regard it as difficult, for it is but a single cry (sayhah wahidah), that is, it is accomplished by a single cry, which is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah). He referred to it as "that" (ha) to indicate the complete connection between the two, as if it were the very same thing. It has also been said that "hiya" (it) refers back to "al-radifah" (the one following), so the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 14:

﴿Then, behold, they will be on the sahirah (the wakeful ground).﴾ "Then" (hina'idhin) here explains the sequence of the return (al-karrah) following the call (al-zajrah) suddenly: that is, "then behold, they are alive upon the surface of the earth after they had been dead in its belly." According to the first interpretation, it explains their presence at the place of standing (al-mawqif) immediately after the return, which he has expressed by the zajrah.

Al-sahirah is the white, level earth, and it was so named because the mirage (al-sarab) flows over it, from their saying "'ayn sahirah" meaning a spring of flowing water, whose opposite is "na'imah" (sleeping). It was also said: it is so named because whoever travels across it does not sleep, out of fear of perishing. It was also said: it is a name for Hell (Jahannam). Al-Raghib said: it is the surface of the earth. It was also said: it is the earth of the Resurrection.

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that al-sahirah is an earth of silver upon which Allah the Exalted was never disobeyed; He created it at that time. It was also said: it is an earth which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will renew on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: it is the name of the seventh earth, which Allah the Exalted will bring forth, and upon which He will call the creatures to account, and that is when the earth will be changed into another earth. Al-Thawri said: al-sahirah is the land of Syria. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: it is the mountain of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said: al-sahirah in the sense of the desert at the edge of Hell.

And His, the Exalted's, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 15:

﴿Has there come to you the story of Moses?﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʼnaf), sent down to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over the denial of his people, by informing him that they will be struck with the like of what befell those who were stronger than them and greater than them. (p-99)

As for the meaning of "Has there come to you": if this is considered the first time that the story of Moses came to him (peace and blessings be upon him), then it is an encouragement for him (peace and blessings be upon him) to listen to his story, as if it were said: "Has his story come to you? I will inform you of it." And if its coming before this is considered, which is what is most apparent from the brevity in relating it, then it is a way of bringing him (peace and blessings be upon him) to acknowledge a matter he already knows beforehand, as if it were said: "Has not his story already come to you?"

And His, the Exalted's, statement:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 16:

﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa﴾ This is an adverbial clause (zarf) modifying the "narration" (al-hadith), not the "coming" (al-ityan), because the two occur at different times.

﴿Tuwa﴾ With a damma on the ta' and without tanwin. It is also read with tanwin (munawwanan), and it is read with a kasra, both with and without tanwin. Whoever reads it with tanwin interprets it as a place name referring to the location (al-makan) rather than the specific piece of ground (al-buq'a). It is also said that it is like Thana, a verbal noun (masdar) of "nada" (to call), or an adjective modifying "al-muqaddas," meaning: He called him twice (nidaina), or "al-muqaddas" [is repeated] once after another time.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 79, verse 17:**

﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾ on the assumption of an implied verb of saying. It is also said that it explains the call (al-nida', the act of calling out), meaning: he called him, "Go." It is also said that it is with the omission of the explanatory "an" (أنِ al-mufassira, the interpretive "an"), and what supports this is the reading of ʿAbd Allah: (أنِ اذْهَبْ) "an idhhab," because the call carries the meaning of saying.

﴿Indeed he has transgressed﴾ is a justification (ta'lil, giving the reason) for the command, or for the obligation to comply with it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 18:

﴿So say﴾ after you have come to him.

﴿Is there in you﴾ a desire and an inclination.

﴿To purify yourself﴾ by omitting one of the two taa's, from tatazakka, i.e., that you purify yourself from the filth of disbelief and transgression. It is also read as (tazzakka) with the shaddah (tashdid).

**"And I will guide you to your Lord"**: and I will direct you to knowing Him, mighty and majestic, so that you come to know Him.

**"So that you fear [Him]"**: since *khashyah* (awe-filled fear of God) cannot occur except after knowing Him, exalted is He. The Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾. Making fear the goal of guidance is because it is the foundation of the matter. Whoever fears God, every good comes from him, and whoever feels secure becomes bold in every evil. Upon him be blessings and peace, he was commanded to address [Pharaoh] with a question whose meaning is an offer (*'ard*), so as to invite him with gentleness of speech and to bring him down from his arrogance through conciliation. This is a detailing of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So speak to him gently, perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾. And the *fa'* (the particle "so") in the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 20:

﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾. The *fa* here is *fasīḥah* (an explanatory particle), which reveals omitted clauses, since their detail is left to be stated in other surahs. The peace and blessings of Allah be upon him did not show him this sign at the outset of the matter. Rather, after what took place between him and Allah Most High, including the request and the response and other exchanges, and after what took place between him and Pharaoh, including the dialogues, until Pharaoh said: ﴿If you have brought a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful﴾. The "showing" (*ir'ā*) may mean either causing to see (*tabṣīr*) or making known (*ta'rīf*). When the accursed one saw it, he recognized it. His claim that it was sorcery was only a display on his part and a show of defiance. Attributing it to him, peace be upon him, is according to outward appearance, just as its attribution to the royal "we" (*nūn al-'aẓamah*, the plural of majesty) in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We had indeed shown him Our signs﴾ is according to reality. The "greatest sign" means the turning of the staff into a serpent, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, for it was the foremost and principal sign, and the others were like its followers. Or both together are meant, which is the view of Mujahid, for they are like one sign. He referred to them in the plural form when He said: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾, in consideration of the wondrous matters within them, each of which is a clear sign ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, as in surah Ta-Ha. It is not admissible to interpret it as the totality of his miracles, for the nine signs other than these two only appeared at his hand, peace be upon him, after he overcame the sorcerers gradually over about twenty years, as passed in surah al-A'raf. There is no doubt that this is the beginning of the story, and the matter of the sorcerers is yet to come.

﴿So he denied﴾ Moses, peace be upon him, and called his miracles sorcery.

﴿And disobeyed﴾ Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by rebelling after he knew the command was true and obedience was obligatory, which is the most severe and the most reprehensible disobedience, since he dared to deny the existence of the Lord of the worlds altogether. The accursed one and his people were commanded to worship Him, Mighty and Majestic, and to abandon the grandiosity that the tyrant claimed and that his rebellious faction accepted from him, not merely to send the Children of Israel free from captivity and oppression.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 22:

﴿Then he turned his back﴾, i.e., he turned away from obedience, or he withdrew from the assembly.

﴿Striving﴾, i.e., he exerted himself in opposing the sign. Alternatively, the sense is: "then he came forward" (thumma aqbal), meaning he began to strive. The phrase "adbar" (turned his back) was put in its place to avoid describing him with coming forward (al-iqbal). It was also said: he turned his back fleeing from the serpent. For it is narrated that when he (peace be upon him) threw down the staff, it turned into a serpent (thu'ban) of great size, its hair bristling, its mouth gaping between its jaws, eighty cubits in length; it placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace, then it advanced toward Pharaoh, who fled and defecated, and the people were routed, crowding one another, so that twenty-five thousand of his people died. It was also said: when it turned into a living serpent, it rose into the sky about a mile, then descended, coming toward Pharaoh, and it began to say: "O Moses, command me with whatever you wish," while Pharaoh said: "I implore you by the One who sent you to take it!" So he took it and it returned to being a staff. Against this is the fact that that occurred before the insistence upon denial and disobedience and the confrontation with the miracle, as his words, may He be exalted, indicate:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 23:**

﴿فَحَشَرَ﴾ *(then he gathered)*, that is, he gathered the sorcerers, in accordance with his saying: "Then Pharaoh sent into the cities to gather [people]." His saying, exalted is He: "So Pharaoh turned away and gathered his scheming," means: what is plotted with, namely the sorcerers and their instruments. It has been said: his troops. It is also permissible that what is meant is all the people.

﴿فَنادى﴾ *(then he called out)* at the assembly, either personally or through a herald.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 24:

﴿فَقالَ أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ It is said: he stood among them as a preacher and said, "That great [claim]."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 79, verse 25:**

﴿So Allah seized him, as an exemplary punishment (nakal) for the Hereafter and the former life.﴾ *Nakal* has the sense of *tankil* (exemplary punishment), as *salam* has the sense of *taslim* (greeting). It is the punishment that makes an exemplary example of whoever sees it or hears of it and prevents him from engaging in what leads to it. Its position is accusative (*nasb*) as an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkad*) like "*wa'da Allah*" (the promise of Allah) and "*sibghata Allah*" (the colouring of Allah). It is as if it were said: "Allah made an example of him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the former life." This is burning in the Hereafter and drowning in this world. It was also said that it is a verbal noun for *akhadha* (seized), meaning: "Allah seized him with the seizing of the punishment of the Hereafter and the former life..." etc. It was also said that it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), meaning: "He seized him for the sake of the punishment..." etc. It was also said that it is in the accusative by elision of the preposition (*naza' al-khafid*), meaning: "He seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the former life." Its attribution to the two abodes is based on the seizing itself occurring in both, not on the basis that the sense of deterrence within it occurs in both, for that cannot be imagined in the Hereafter; rather, it occurs in this world, since the otherworldly punishment certainly makes an example of whoever hears of it and prevents him from engaging in what leads to it. It was also said that what is meant by "the Hereafter and the former life" is His saying: "I am your Lord, the Most High," and His saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than Me﴾. It was said that there were forty years between the two statements, so the attribution is the attribution of the effect to its cause.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 26:

﴿Indeed, in that⦆ i.e., in what has been mentioned of the story of Pharaoh, and what he did, and what was done to him.

﴿is truly a lesson⦆ a great one.

﴿for those who fear⦆ i.e., for those whose nature it is to fear, and this is the one whose nature is to have knowledge (ma'rifah). And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 27:

﴿Are you the more difficult to create?﴾ This is an address to the people of Makkah who denied the Resurrection, on the basis of their own assumption that it is difficult, by way of rebuke and silencing them, after the perfect ease of it in relation to the power of God Most High has been made clear by His saying, Most High: ﴿Then it is but a single shout﴾. That is: Is your creation after your death more difficult? That is: more arduous and harder in your estimation.

﴿Or the sky?﴾ That is: or the creation of the sky, with its greatness and its containing of wondrous marvels whose minutest aspects the intellects are bewildered to observe, as in His saying, Most High: ﴿Certainly the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾, and His saying, Most High: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾, and His saying, Most High: ﴿He built it﴾ ... etc. This is an explanation and elaboration of the manner of its creation, which is implied by His saying "or ﴿the sky﴾". The omission of the agent in it and in the verbs coordinated with it is, to the extent that it draws attention to His being definitively the agent and to the magnification of His majestic status, glorious and exalted, something that is not hidden. And His saying, Most High:

**"He raised its vault (samk)"**: an explanation of the building. That is, He made the measure of its height above the earth, and its extension toward the direction of elevation, long and lofty, a journey of five hundred years.

**"Then He leveled it"**: He made it even and smooth, without unevenness or fissures; or He completed it with what He knew it would be completed by, namely the stars, the epicycles (tada'wir) and other things that none knows but the Creator, the All-Knowing. This is from their saying "sawwā amra fulānin" (he set someone's affair in order) when he put it right.

﴿And He made its night dark﴾, i.e., He made it dark. It is said: "ghatasha al-layl" and "aghtashahu Allah ta'ala," just as it is said: "zalama" and "azlamahu." This was already discussed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when it grows dark over them, they stand still﴾. It is also said: "aghtasha al-layl," just as it is said: "azlama."

﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾, i.e., He brought forth its daylight. He expressed it by the forenoon (duha) because it is the most noble and the most pleasant of its times, so it was most deserving of mention in the context of bestowing favour. This is the secret of mentioning it after the night and of expressing its origination by "bringing forth," for the bestowal of light after darkness is more complete in favour (p. 102) and more perfect in beneficence. The attribution of the night and the forenoon to the heaven is because their occurrence revolves around its motion. It is also permissible that the attribution of the forenoon to it be through the sun, i.e., He brought forth the light of its sun, and it was expressed as the forenoon because it is the time when its sovereignty stands and its brightness is at full.

﴿And the earth, after that, He spread out (dahaha)﴾, meaning: He extended it and made it level for its inhabitants to dwell in and to move about in its regions. The accusative of "al-ard" (the earth) is by a suppressed verb which "dahaha" explains.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 31:

﴿He brought forth from it its water﴾, by causing springs to gush forth from it and rivers to flow.

﴿And its pasture﴾, i.e., its grazing. Originally it is a noun of place (mawdi' al-ri'y), the place where animals graze. It has also been said that it is a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi) with the meaning of a passive participle (maf'ul), i.e., "that which is grazed."

The sentence is left without a conjunction (tajrid al-jumlah 'an al-'atif), either because it is an explanation and elaboration (bayan wa tafsir) of "He spread it out" (dahaha) and a completion of it, for settlement (sukna) cannot be achieved merely by spreading out and leveling the ground; rather, the arrangement of the means of livelihood, of food and drink, is necessarily required. Or because it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject (fa'il), with "qad" implied according to the majority (al-Jumhur), or without it according to the Kufans and al-Akhfash, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿Or they come to you with their hearts restricted﴾ (Qur'an 4:90).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 32:

﴿Wal-jibāla﴾ (and the mountains) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that the following verb explains.

﴿Arsāhā﴾ means: He established them (al-jibāl), and by them He established the earth so that it would not shake with its inhabitants. This is a confirmation of the truth and an alert that the "anchoring" (al-rusuww) attributed to them in many places of the revelation, by describing them as "the firm mountains" (al-rawāsī), is not something required by their own essences. Rather, it is by the anchoring of the Mighty and Majestic; had it not been for Him, they would not have been stable in themselves, let alone have stabilized the earth. It has also been read as (wal-ardu wal-jibālu) with the nominative, as a new sentence (ibtidā'). Perhaps the mention of bringing forth water and pasture is placed first, though anchoring precedes it in existence, to show the complete concern with the matter of food and drink, and to remove the suspicion that the pronouns of "water" and "pasture" refer back to the mountains. As you see, this apparently indicates that the spreading of the earth (dahw al-ard) came after the creation of the heaven and what is in it. This is what has been related from al-Hasan: that He, exalted is He, created the earth at the site of Bayt al-Maqdis like a grinding stone, with smoke clinging to it. Then He raised the smoke, created the heavens from it, held the stone in its place, and spread out the earth from it. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Were the heavens and the earth a closed-up mass, then We ripped them apart﴾ (21:30), and the verse continues. It has already been mentioned in Surah Ha Mim al-Sajda that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?﴾ (41:9), up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke﴾ (41:11), and the verse continues, indicates, if the creation mentioned there and the three verbs coordinated with it are taken in their apparent meanings and not in their implied sense, that this and what is in Surah al-Baqara, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth, then He turned to the heaven and fashioned them as seven heavens﴾ (2:29), both indicate that the creation of the earth and what is in it preceded the creation of the heaven. This is the position of the majority of the exegetes. It has also been related that the Throne was upon the water before the creation of the heavens and the earth. Then He caused agitation in the water, so it foamed, and smoke rose from it. As for the foam, it remained on the surface of the water, and from it He created dryness and made it one earth; then He split it and made it into earths. As for the smoke, it rose and ascended, and from it He created the heavens. It has also been related that He created the body of the earth on Sunday and Monday and spread it out, and created what is in it on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens and what is in them on Thursday and Friday, and created Adam, peace be upon him, in the last hour of it, which is the hour in which the Hour will take place. Therefore the closest interpretation of this verse, as has been said, is that the reference is to what has been mentioned of the building of the heaven, raising its height, shaping it, and other things, not to the heaven itself, and that the sequence is in mention, as is customary in the speech of Arabs and non-Arabs, not in existence. This is because, as you have learned, the accusative status of the earth is by an implied verb placed before it, which has been omitted by way of the rule of explanation, not by what is mentioned after it, in order to convey restriction, and so the sequence in existence is fixed. The benefit of delaying it in mention is either to alert that it is insufficient in indicating the overwhelming power in relation to the states of the heaven, or to indicate that it is more involved in obligation, since the benefits tied to what is in the earth are greater, the welfare of people is more evidently connected to it, and their comprehensive knowledge of its details is more complete. What has been related from al-Hasan is not an explicit text on the earth's spreading being after the creation of the heaven, since the spreading of the earth is coordinated with the sending up of the smoke and the creation of the heaven by the conjunction "wa" (and), which has no indication of order. This is on the assumption that what is mentioned in the verses of Surah al-Sajda of creation, and the three verbs coordinated with it, are taken in their apparent meanings. But if they are taken in their implied sense, there is no indication in them except the precedence of the implied determination of the earth and what is in it over the bringing into existence of the heaven. Likewise, there is no indication of order at all if the word "thumma" (then) in them and in what is in Surah al-Baqara is taken to mean delay in rank. The detailed discussion has already passed in the mentioned surah. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 33:

﴿A provision for you and for your cattle.﴾ It may be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the object indicating the reason for an action), meaning: He did that as a provision (tamti'an) for you and for your cattle, because the benefit of what has been mentioned of spreading out (al-bast), making it level (al-tamhid), and bringing forth water and pasture (al-mar'a) reaches them and their cattle. The intended meaning of "pasture" (al-mar'a) is that which encompasses what a human eats and other than that, based on the metaphorical extension (isti'ara) of grazing (al-ra'y) to the consumption of food in general, like the metaphor of al-marsan (the nose of an animal) for the human nose. It has also been said: it is an infinitive (masdar) emphasizing its implied verb, meaning: He gave you enjoyment with that as enjoyment, or it is an infinitive not from its own verb, since the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ has the meaning of "He gave enjoyment with that." And the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 34:

﴿Then when the Great Calamity comes﴾. That is: the greatest disaster, which overwhelms (taммa) all other calamities, meaning it rises above them and overpowers them. It is the Resurrection (al-Qiyama), or the Second Blast (al-Nafkha al-Thaniya). It has also been said: it is the Hour when creatures are driven to their place of gathering (mahshar). And it has been said: it is the Hour when the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of Hellfire to Hellfire. This begins the explanation of the states of their final return, following the explanation of the states of their worldly life in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿as an enjoyment for you﴾ ... etc. The fa' (then) indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it after a short while, as the word "enjoyment" (mata', al-mata') itself suggests.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 35:

﴿On the Day when man will remember what he strove for﴾. It is said: it is a substitute (badal) for "when it comes" (idha ja'at). The more evident view is that it is in the accusative, governed by "I mean" (a'ni), as it is said: an explanation (tafsir) of "the greatest calamity" (al-tamma al-kubra). For substituting from it with a pure adverbial noun (zarf mahd) weakens its connection to the response (jawab). It is also permissible that it be a substitute for "the greatest calamity," marked with a fatha because it is attached to a verb, according to the opinion of the Kufans: that is, on that Day every person will remember what he did of good or evil, by seeing it recorded in the scroll of his deeds, which he had forgotten because of extreme heedlessness and the long passage of time, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has counted it, while they have forgotten it﴾. It is also permissible that "ma" be a verbal noun (masdariyya).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 36:

﴿And the Hellfire is made manifest﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "came" (in the preceding verse), meaning: it is displayed in a clear manifestation that is hidden from no one. ﴿For whoever sees﴾, whoever he may be. It is related that it will be uncovered, so it blazes, and every person with sight will see it. It is also read: (wa-burrizat) with the light form (takhfif), and "li-man ra'a" and "li-man tara" are taken as referring to the pronoun in "fihi" (in it), referring to the Hellfire, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when it sees them from a distant place﴾. And it is taken as addressed to the Messenger of God ﷺ, meaning: you did not see it from among the disbelievers. And His saying, exalted is He:

**﴿Then as for him who transgressed﴾ ... and so on.** This is the answer (jawab) to ﴿And when the Great Calamity comes﴾, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there comes to you guidance from Me...﴾ the verse. It was also said that it is an elaboration (tafsil) of a deleted answer, its estimated meaning being: "The beholders were divided into two groups: as for him who..." and so on. What the majesty of the revelation calls for, and what the context of awe-inspiring terror requires, is that the deleted answer was of such great matters as eyes have not witnessed, as passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when God gathers the Messengers﴾ (5:109). That is: "Then as for him who transgressed, rebelled against obedience, and exceeded the limit in disobedience."

Translation:

﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾, the transient one, which is on the wing of passing away; so he became absorbed in what he was given enjoyment of therein, and did not prepare himself for the everlasting life of the Hereafter through faith and obedience.

**Verse 39 (Surah al-Nazi'at, 79):** ﴿فَإنَّ الجحيم﴾ — "Then indeed, Hellfire" — the one whose matter has been mentioned.

﴿هِيَ المَأْوى﴾ — "it is the refuge." That is, it is his refuge (*ma'wa*). The *lam* (in *al-ma'wa*) stands in place of the possessive construction (*idafa*), because it is known that the owner of the refuge is the tyrant (*taghi*), as in your saying: "Lower the gaze" (*ghuddu al-tarf*). The entry of the *lam* on *al-ma'wa* and *al-taraf* is for definiteness, since both are well known. As for *huwa* (*hiya*), it is either a *damir al-fasl* (separator pronoun) or a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). It was said: the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr and his father al-Harith, who were famous for their extremity in disbelief and transgression.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 40:

﴿And as for he who feared the standing before his Lord﴾ i.e., his standing before the Master of his affair on the Great Calamity, the day when man will remember what he strove for.

﴿and restrained the soul from desire﴾ from inclining toward it by virtue of the human natural disposition (jibillah). He did not give weight to the enjoyment of worldly life and its splendor, nor was he deceived by its adornments and embellishments, knowing well the dire consequence of these things.

﴿Then indeed Paradise is the refuge﴾, for him and not for anyone else. It is also said that the two verses were revealed concerning Abu 'Aziz ibn 'Umayr and Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr. Mus'ab had killed his brother Abu 'Aziz on the Day of Uhud, and he protected the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he was martyred, may Allah be pleased with him. That said, it has also been said that the response (jawab) of "idha" ("when") is what indicates it, namely the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿On the day when man will remember⦆ ... etc. The meaning is: when the Great Catastrophe comes, man will remember what he strove for, in the manner of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾ and His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and left behind﴾. Then His words, "and Hellfire will be brought forth" (wa-burrizat al-jahim), are a coordination (ʿaṭf) upon it. The use of the past tense (ṣīghat al-māḍī) is to indicate certainty. Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to man, with "qad" implied or not implied, according to the two opinions. For the one who holds the view that it does not require a returning pronoun (ʿāʾid), it needs no ʿāʾid. As for His words: ﴿But as for one who transgressed﴾ ... etc., they are a detailed explanation of the two states of the man who remembers what he strove for, and a division of him, according to his deeds, into the two categories mentioned.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 42:

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will be its arrival?﴾ "Its arrival" (mursaha, from irsa'), that is, its establishment. They ask when Allah the Exalted will establish it, make it firm, and bring it into being. It has also been said: "When" (ayyan) refers to the time of its endpoint and its resting place, just as the anchorage (mursa) of a ship is the place where it comes to an end and comes to rest. And His statement, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 43:

﴿Why [should] you [be] of mentioning it?﴾ This is a denial and a rejection of the question of the polytheists about it, meaning: in what matter are you one who mentions to them its time and informs them of it, so that they ask you to clarify it? Like His saying, exalted is He: "They ask you as though you were well-informed about it" (7:187), meaning: you are in no way [one who] mentions it to them or clarifies its time; for that would be a branch of your knowledge of it, and how could you have that, when it is among what Allah, the Knower of the Unseen, has kept exclusively to His knowledge? Whoever says, by way of giving a reason: "Indeed, mentioning it only increases them in misguidance (ghayy)," has strayed far from the truth. It has also been said that "Why" is a denial of their question, and what follows it is a resumptive (isti'naf) clause giving the reason for the denial and an explanation of the invalidity of the question, meaning: why is this question [asked]? Then it begins: "You are [a sign] of its [approach]," meaning: your sending, and you are the Seal of the Prophets, sent at the breath of the Hour, a sign among its signs and an indication guiding them to knowledge of its occurrence in the near future. So this degree of knowledge is sufficient for them. Thus the meaning of His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 44:

﴿To your Lord belongs its finality.﴾ On this reading, the ultimate knowledge of it returns to Him, exalted is He, meaning: knowledge of its reality (kunh) and the details of its matter, and the time of its occurrence, belongs to no one other than Him. Their duty is only to know its nearness and imminence, and that has already been achieved by your being sent (mab'ath), so what is the point of their asking about it after that? As for the first reading, its meaning is: to Him, exalted is He, is the termination of its knowledge; none of creation has any share in it, whoever he may be. So why do they ask you about it? And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 45:

﴿Verily you are only a warner to him who fears it.﴾ On the first interpretation, it confirms what comes before it, His saying, "What have you to do with mentioning it?", and clarifies what is meant by it and states the duty of the Messenger, upon him be peace and blessings (ﷺ), in that matter. Denying that he (ﷺ) has any part in mentioning it may give the outward impression that he (ﷺ) has no right to mention it in any way at all. This is removed by explaining that what is negated of him (ﷺ) is mentioning it to them by specifying its time, as they used to ask him (ﷺ) about it. So the meaning is: "You are only a warner to him who fears it. Your duty is to comply with what you have been commanded: explaining its nearness and detailing the various kinds of terrors within it, as you know through information. It is not your duty to specify its time, which has not been entrusted to you. So why do they ask you about what is not among your duties to explain?" On the second interpretation, it confirms His saying, "What have you to do with mentioning it?", by showing that his being sent, upon him be peace and blessings (ﷺ), while he is the Seal of the Prophets, upon them be peace, is a warning of the coming of the Hour, as his saying (ﷺ) expresses: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two, [the Hour] almost outstripping me." It has been read as (مُنْذِرٌ) with tanwin (nunation), which is the original form, and the idafa (construct phrase, i.e., "warner of him who fears") is a lightened form that is suitable for the present and the future. When the past is intended, the idafa becomes necessary. The restriction of the warning to "him who fears" despite the generality of the call is because he is the one who benefits from it. And His, may He be exalted, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 79, verse 46:

﴿As if they had not remained but an evening or its morning.﴾ This is either a confirmation and emphasis of what the warning (al-indhar) implies about how quickly the thing warned of would come, especially on the second interpretation. That is, "as if they, on the day they see it, had not remained after being warned of it except for one day's evening or its morning." Then, since the day was dropped, its morning was attributed to its evening. Or it is a response to what was incorporated into their question. They were asking about it in a manner of impatience, urging it on, though in the manner of mockery toward it, saying: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" So the meaning is: "as if they, on the day they see it, had not remained after the threat," confirming the warning and rejecting their impatience. On the first interpretation, the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun, since in both readings of the idafa (construction) and its absence, it is the object of "mundhir" (warner). Just as the saying of the Exalted, ﴿as if they had not remained but an hour of the day﴾, is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the object in "yahshuruhum" (He will gather them), meaning: He will gather them, resembling those who did not remain in the world except for an hour. Except that the resemblance there is in the apparent states of dress and appearance, while in what we are discussing it is in belief. As if it were said: "You warn them, resembling, on the day they see it, in belief, those who did not remain after the warning of it except for that brief period." On the second interpretation, it is a resumed clause (mustanfa'a) with no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis).

It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites surah al-Nazi'at, he will be among those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will detain in the grave and on the Day of Resurrection until he enters Paradise, for the duration of an obligatory prayer."

And Allah knows best.
